description: Hard-difficulty practice set (20 questions) covering: Anatomy, Fundamentals of Electro Therapy, Fundamentals of Exercise Therapy, General Surgery & Orthopedics, OBGY, Pathology & Microbiology, Physiology, Physiotherapy in Community Health, Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition, Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition, Physiotherapy in Neurosciences, Psychiatry.

questions.question: Dislocation of the lunate bone (from a fall on the acutely dorsiflexed hand) typically displaces it in which direction, and can mimic the features of which condition?

options.A: Displaces posteriorly; mimics De Quervain's tenosynovitis
options.B: Displaces anteriorly; can produce carpal tunnel syndrome-like features
options.C: Displaces laterally; mimics ulnar nerve palsy at the elbow
options.D: Does not displace, only rotates in place with no clinical effect

questions.explanation: Dislocation of the lunate is produced by a fall on the acutely dorsiflexed hand with the elbow flexed; it displaces the lunate anteriorly, where it can compress the median nerve within the carpal tunnel, producing carpal tunnel syndrome-like features.
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Upper Limb
questions.sourceChapter: Bones of the Upper Limb — Carpal Bones, Clinical Anatomy
questions.subject: Anatomy

questions.question: The Nernst equation is used in physiology to calculate:

options.A: The equilibrium potential for a specific ion, based on its concentration gradient across the membrane
options.B: The total resting metabolic rate of a cell
options.C: The rate of action potential propagation along an axon
options.D: The molecular weight of an ion

questions.explanation: The Nernst equation calculates the equilibrium potential for a given ion — the membrane potential at which the electrical force on that ion exactly balances its concentration gradient, so there is no net movement of that ion across the membrane.
questions.sourceChapter: The Membrane Potentials — The Equilibrium Potential
questions.subject: Physiology

questions.question: Among the TORCH agents, which one is most harmful to the fetus specifically when acquired during the first 10 weeks of pregnancy?

options.A: Cytomegalovirus
options.B: Toxoplasma
options.C: Rubella
options.D: Herpes simplex virus

questions.explanation: Rubella (German measles) is teratogenic, and infection during the acute stage of the first 10 weeks of pregnancy is far more harmful to the fetus than infection later in gestation, producing the classic congenital rubella syndrome (ocular defects, cardiac defects, CNS manifestations, sensorineural deafness).
questions.sourceChapter: Infectious and Parasitic Diseases — TORCH Complex
questions.subject: Pathology & Microbiology

questions.question: In MS, a 'dyssynergic' bladder refers to a problem where:

options.A: The bladder is simply too small to store any urine
options.B: There is a coordination problem between bladder (detrusor) contraction and sphincter relaxation
options.C: The bladder never contracts under any circumstances
options.D: Urine production stops entirely

questions.explanation: A dyssynergic bladder represents a coordination problem between bladder contraction and sphincter relaxation, distinct from a small spastic bladder (failure to store) or a flaccid/big bladder (failure to empty) — both of which are other recognised patterns of MS-related bladder dysfunction.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 16: Multiple Sclerosis — Bladder Dysfunction
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: 'Subinvolution' and 'superinvolution' of the uterus refer respectively to:

options.A: Delayed/incomplete involution, and a smaller-than-normal uterus sometimes seen with continued lactation
options.B: Two names for exactly the same clinical finding
options.C: Involution occurring only in the cervix versus only in the vagina
options.D: Terms with no real clinical distinction from normal involution

questions.explanation: Subinvolution refers to involution proceeding more slowly or incompletely than expected. Superinvolution, by contrast, describes a uterus that becomes smaller than normal, sometimes seen in lactating women — a change that reverses if lactation is withheld.
questions.sourceChapter: Normal Puerperium — Clinical Assessment of Involution
questions.subject: OBGY

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: 'Accommodation' in nerve physiology refers to the phenomenon whereby:

options.A: A nerve becomes permanently unresponsive after any stimulation
options.B: The nerve adapts to a constant current over time, so that an unvarying (unchanging) current becomes ineffective at initiating an impulse
options.C: Muscle fibres physically move position to avoid the electrode
options.D: Only denervated muscle can show accommodation

questions.explanation: Accommodation is the nerve's adaptation to a constant, unvarying current flow through a mechanism not fully understood — as a result, a current that does not change is not effective at initiating a nerve impulse, which is why intermittent or varying currents are needed for electrical stimulation.
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Accommodation
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: Posterior internal impingement of the shoulder, commonly seen in overhead athletes, occurs when the rotator cuff impinges against the posterosuperior edge of the glenoid, with the arm positioned in:

options.A: Abduction, extension, and lateral rotation
options.B: Full adduction and medial rotation
options.C: Complete elbow flexion with the shoulder neutral
options.D: Full flexion with the forearm pronated

questions.explanation: Posterior internal impingement occurs when the arm is abducted, extended, and laterally rotated — a position common in the late cocking phase of throwing — causing the rotator cuff to impinge against the posterosuperior glenoid rim, sometimes producing a 'kissing' labral lesion.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 5: Shoulder — Posterior Internal Impingement Test
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: How does the metabolic response to trauma/sepsis differ from simple starvation regarding ketone formation?

options.A: Both produce identical, unimpaired ketone formation
options.B: In trauma/sepsis, ketone formation is impaired, and glucose-generating protein breakdown cannot be entirely prevented even by giving glucose
options.C: Trauma always increases ketone formation far beyond that seen in starvation
options.D: Ketone formation is irrelevant to both conditions

questions.explanation: Unlike simple starvation (where glucose administration can readily reverse protein catabolism), trauma and sepsis patients have impaired ketone formation, and gluconeogenesis (protein breakdown to make glucose) cannot be entirely prevented by giving exogenous glucose — a key nutritional distinction between the two states.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Nutrition and Fluid Therapy — Metabolic Response to Trauma and Sepsis
questions.subject: General Surgery & Orthopedics

questions.question: A diagnosis of multiple sclerosis (MS) requires evidence of CNS damage that satisfies which two key criteria?

options.A: Damage in only one CNS location, confirmed once
options.B: Dissemination of lesions in space (at least two separate CNS areas) AND dissemination in time (damage at two separate points at least 1 month apart)
options.C: A single MRI scan showing any abnormality
options.D: Positive family history alone, without any imaging

questions.explanation: MS diagnosis requires evidence of damage in at least two separate areas of the CNS (dissemination in space) occurring at two separate points in time at least 1 month apart (dissemination in time), plus exclusion of other possible diagnoses — as reflected in the revised McDonald Criteria.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 16: Multiple Sclerosis — Diagnosis
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: In the rehabilitation framework for MS, which category of impairment is described as generally NOT responsive to intervention, in contrast to indirect impairments caused by inactivity/disuse (which CAN be modified)?

options.A: Direct CNS impairments (from the disease process itself)
options.B: Decreased muscle endurance from disuse
options.C: Osteoporosis from inactivity
options.D: Cardiovascular deconditioning

questions.explanation: Direct CNS impairments caused by the MS disease process itself are not responsive to rehabilitative intervention, whereas INDIRECT impairments from inactivity and disuse (decreased muscle endurance, osteoporosis, cardiovascular deconditioning) can be meaningfully improved — for example, strength training can improve balance and gait despite the underlying CNS damage remaining unchanged.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 16: Multiple Sclerosis — Framework for Rehabilitation
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: Exclusive breastfeeding provides approximately what level of contraceptive protection for the first 6 months postpartum?

options.A: About 20%
options.B: About 50%
options.C: About 98%
options.D: 0% — breastfeeding provides no contraceptive effect

questions.explanation: In a woman who is exclusively breastfeeding, lactational amenorrhoea provides approximately 98% contraceptive protection for up to 6 months postpartum — a recognised natural method of contraception, though ovulation can occasionally precede the return of menstruation.
questions.sourceChapter: Normal Puerperium — Menstruation and Ovulation
questions.subject: OBGY

questions.question: Functionally, the iliotibial tract's main role during standing with slightly flexed knees (e.g. leaning forward) is to:

options.A: Provide the main support of the knee against gravity, stabilizing it in extension and partial flexion
options.B: Flex the knee actively against resistance
options.C: Provide sensation to the anterior thigh only
options.D: Have no functional role in standing or walking

questions.explanation: The iliotibial tract stabilizes the knee in both extension and partial flexion, and is used constantly during walking and running. When leaning forward with slightly flexed knees, it becomes the main support of the knee against gravity.
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Lower Limb
questions.sourceChapter: Front of Thigh — Iliotibial Tract
questions.subject: Anatomy

questions.question: How is musculoskeletal (chest wall) pain typically distinguished from pleuritic pain on physical examination?

options.A: Musculoskeletal pain is reproduced by palpation, while pleuritic pain is not
options.B: Both are always identical and cannot be distinguished clinically
options.C: Pleuritic pain is always reproduced by palpation, musculoskeletal pain never is
options.D: Musculoskeletal pain never worsens with movement

questions.explanation: Musculoskeletal (chest wall) pain is usually well localized and its reproduction on palpation is a key distinguishing clinical feature — pleuritic pain, by contrast, is not reproduced by palpation.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.sourceChapter: Assessment — Chest Pain
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: John Watson's famous 1920 'Little Albert' experiment is cited in psychiatry textbooks as historical evidence for which theory of phobia causation?

options.A: Psychodynamic theory (displacement)
options.B: Behavioural theory (classical conditioning)
options.C: Biological/genetic theory
options.D: Biochemical serotonin theory

questions.explanation: Watson experimentally produced a phobia of white objects in an infant ('Little Albert') by repeatedly pairing a neutral white object with a loud, frightening noise — a classic demonstration of classical conditioning supporting the behavioural theory that phobias are learned, conditioned fear responses.
questions.sourceBook: Ahuja, A Short Textbook of Psychiatry
questions.sourceChapter: Neurotic, Stress-related and Somatoform Disorders — Phobic Disorder, Aetiology
questions.subject: Psychiatry

questions.question: The hallmark microscopic feature of coagulative necrosis is:

options.A: Complete liquefaction with no recognisable cell outlines
options.B: Preservation of the basic outline of the cell ('tombstones') even though cytoplasmic and nuclear detail is lost
options.C: Cheese-like, structureless material with surrounding granulomatous inflammation
options.D: Formation of calcium soaps from adipocyte breakdown

questions.explanation: In coagulative necrosis, cells are converted into 'tombstones' — their outline and cell type remain recognisable even though the cytoplasmic and nuclear details are lost; unlike liquefactive necrosis, cell digestion and liquefaction do not occur.
questions.sourceChapter: Cell Injury, Cellular Adaptations and Cellular Ageing — Coagulative Necrosis
questions.subject: Pathology & Microbiology

questions.question: The External Rotation Recurvatum Test, in which the examiner lifts both of the patient's big toes off the table and observes for relative hyperextension and lateral tibial rotation on the affected side, is a test for:

options.A: Posterolateral rotary instability in extension
options.B: Meniscal tear
options.C: Patellofemoral pain syndrome
options.D: Iliotibial band tightness

questions.explanation: The External Rotation Recurvatum Test assesses for posterolateral rotary instability in extension — a positive test shows the affected knee falling into relative hyperextension (genu varum appearance) with lateral tibial rotation due to gravity, when both legs are lifted by the toes.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 12: Knee — External Rotation Recurvatum Test
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: In epidemiological terminology, a 'variate' that can only be present or absent (e.g. lung cancer, a broken leg) is described as:

options.A: Continuously distributed
options.B: Discrete
options.C: A circumstance, not a variate
options.D: Non-measurable and therefore not usable in epidemiology

questions.explanation: A variate (any piece of information about a patient or their disease) can be discrete — present or absent, like lung cancer or a broken leg — or continuously distributed, like blood pressure, serum cholesterol, or height. A 'circumstance' is a distinct concept: any environmental factor suspected of causing a disease, such as air pollution.
questions.sourceBook: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Epidemiology and Epidemiologic Methods — Basic Measurements in Epidemiology
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Community Health

questions.question: In arthrometer testing, the 'quadriceps active position' refers to the knee angle at which:

options.A: The tibia shows no forward movement when the quadriceps contracts, typically around 70° of flexion
options.B: The knee is fully extended at 0°
options.C: The patient is asked to relax completely with no muscle contraction
options.D: The hamstrings are maximally contracted instead of the quadriceps

questions.explanation: The quadriceps neutral (active) angle is the knee flexion angle — typically around 70° — at which an isolated quadriceps contraction produces no anterior tibial translation in a normal knee; this position is used as a reference when testing the injured knee for abnormal anterior displacement (suggestive of PCL injury).
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 12: Knee — Quadriceps Neutral Test
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: Kleine-Levin syndrome, a rare recurrent hypersomnia, classically also includes which additional feature?

options.A: Hyperphagia (voracious appetite)
options.B: Complete loss of appetite
options.C: Permanent memory loss
options.D: Total insomnia between episodes

questions.explanation: Kleine-Levin syndrome is classically characterised by recurrent hypersomnia (always present) along with hyperphagia (usually present, a voracious appetite), and sometimes hypersexuality — predominantly affecting males with onset in the second decade of life.
questions.sourceBook: Ahuja, A Short Textbook of Psychiatry
questions.sourceChapter: Sleep Disorders — Kleine-Levin Syndrome
questions.subject: Psychiatry

questions.question: A 'pseudomyostatic' (apparent) contracture, as distinguished from a true myostatic contracture, is primarily caused by:

options.A: An actual reduction in the number of sarcomeres arranged in series within the muscle
options.B: Hypertonicity such as spasticity or rigidity following a CNS lesion, which can be temporarily reduced with neuromuscular inhibition techniques
options.C: Intra-articular adhesions and joint effusion
options.D: Replacement of normal muscle tissue with fibrotic scar tissue

questions.explanation: Unlike a true myostatic contracture (adaptive shortening of the muscle-tendon unit itself with no specific muscle pathology), a pseudomyostatic contracture results from ongoing hypertonicity, muscle spasm, or pain — the muscle only appears shortened, and full passive elongation becomes possible again once inhibition techniques temporarily reduce that muscle tension.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 4: Stretching for Impaired Mobility — Types of Contracture
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Exercise Therapy
